results.what: Reduction of oscillation durations to infinitely small arcs for geometrically decaying amplitude: t0 = t − t·a·b·(sinh λ/λ)/(64 r²), with λ = ln(a/b) and amplitudes read in scale divisions at mirror distance r.
results.modern_name: Reduction of pendulum/magnet oscillation period to infinitesimal amplitude (finite-amplitude correction T0(1+α²/16), averaged over exponential damping)
results.usually_credited_to: Amplitude correction: classical, 18th century (Euler, Bernoulli, Borda for pendulums). The damped-arc version is used in Gauss's and Weber's magnetic publications, Intensitas 1832/33 and Resultate des magnetischen Vereins 1836–41.

results.what: Exact logarithmic evaluation of sinh λ/λ as [log(10^{2d} − 1) − d] − log d + log(1/(2 ln10)), used instead of the series when d is large.
results.modern_name: Computation of sinh(x)/x via common logarithms

results.what: Re-indexing amplitude readings by 4 swings using the local logarithmic decrement.
results.usually_credited_to: Routine; the logarithmic decrement was formalized by Gauss and Weber in the 1830s.

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine numerical reductions of magnetometer and torsion oscillation data from the well-documented 1832 Gauss–Weber experiments, using the amplitude-reduction formula that Gauss himself published. The only mildly interesting detail is the neat closed form a·b·sinh(λ)/λ and its exact log evaluation, which is entirely consistent with known Gauss practice.

checkable.asserts: Identity behind the formula: the mean of the squared amplitude under geometric decay equals a*b*sinh(λ)/λ (result is 0 for positive a, b).
The constant 9.33675 equals log10(1/(2 ln 10)) in the +10 convention.
